from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
p.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
texts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 texts.append(f'\\n\\n=== PAGE {i} ===\\n\\n'+page.extract_text())
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print(''.join(texts[:4]))
PY"

strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: combining low-memory adaptation with quantization while producing merged integer weights without a separate floating-point adapter. Freezing the base weights plausibly reduces optimizer storage substantially relative to full-weight QAT.

Table 2 provides encouraging evidence across five LLaMA/LLaMA2 models and two precisions. L4Q improves average commonsense accuracy over GPTQ+LoRA in all ten settings, by 0.8–3.7 percentage points. Its 4-bit results remain within 0.7 points of the corresponding 16-bit LoRA results.

The paper provides an understandable high-level algorithm, important training settings, per-task results, and initialization/quantization-parameter ablations. The reported 33B experiment demonstrates feasibility on one 80GB GPU under the stated 128-token training configuration.
weaknesses: The memory advantage over LoRA is confounded by precision settings and inadequately explained. Reducing optimizer-state precision for 10.1M trainable LoRA parameters cannot alone explain the 54.64-to-25.36GB difference in Table 4. Under the paper’s own BF16 comparison, 33B LoRA uses 69.2GB versus L4Q’s 73.2GB; GPTQ+LoRA uses 19.2GB in Table 1. A matched-precision breakdown of weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states is necessary to establish the claimed savings.

The mathematical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Equations (8)–(9) omit the declared LoRA scaling factor α. In Equation (13), the unclipped scale derivative should depend on (w−b_w)/s_w, whereas the expression omits the learned offset. The initialization parameter γ mentioned in Section 4.1 is also absent from the initialization equations. These may be presentation errors, but the manuscript provides no L4Q implementation link to verify the actual updates.

The comparisons do not adequately establish the claimed training-efficiency advantage. L4Q, GPTQ+LoRA, and QA-LoRA use different training budgets, and QA-LoRA also uses a different quantization group size. Matched-budget learning curves would clarify convergence and final-quality tradeoffs. QA-LoRA is evaluated only on LLaMA 7B commonsense tasks, leaving the strongest comparator absent from larger-model and MMLU evaluations.

The MMLU discussion overstates the evidence. L4Q underperforms GPTQ+LoRA in five of six 5-shot comparisons. For 4-bit LLaMA 7B, its accuracy decreases from 33.5% zero-shot to 32.4% five-shot. These results do not support a general claim of improved few-shot performance and require explicit discussion alongside the stronger commonsense results.

The ablations do not cleanly identify the proposed mechanisms. Table 4 assigns 56.7M versus 113.4M trainable parameters to two allegedly scale-only variants, then reports no parameter increase when adding trainable bias. This inconsistency undermines the initialization comparison. No controlled precision ablation establishes that jointly learning scale and bias enables BF16 stability, and no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of small gains.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: microbatching, gradient accumulation, checkpointing, evaluation versions, and random seeds are unspecified. The evaluation description names CommonsenseQA while Table 2 reports OBQA. Integer weights also provide only prospective acceleration benefits without inference measurements. Corrected method specifications and controlled experiments are needed before a sound Findings recommendation; these revisions appear feasible within the next review cycle.
